name: Losar in Rimbik and the ridge villages
when: Jan–Mar: Tamang Sonam Lhosar, then Sherpa Gyalpo Losar (lunar calendar)
summary: Losar, the Himalayan Buddhist new year, is celebrated in Sherpa and Tamang homes and gompas across the Singalila villages, from Maneybhanjan to Rimbik. Tamang families mark Sonam Lhosar around January–February; Sherpa families mark Gyalpo Losar, the Tibetan new year, around February–March. It is a family festival of visits, food and prayer.
body: The ridge's Buddhist communities count new year by the lunar calendar, and not all on the same day. Tamang families celebrate Sonam Lhosar, which falls on the first day of the bright half of the Nepali month of Magh, usually in late January or February. Sherpa families celebrate Gyalpo Losar, the Tibetan new year, a few weeks later, usually in February or early March. In a mixed town like Rimbik or Maneybhanjan, both may come within a month of each other.

Before Losar, houses are cleaned and new prayer flags raised. On the day and those that follow, families visit the gompa, offer butter lamps and khada scarves, and then visit relatives and neighbours. Tables fill with khapse, the fried pastries made for the new year, along with meat dishes, rice and home-made drinks. Elders are greeted first, and younger people receive blessings.

For a visitor, Losar is a time to watch, not to tour. There are community gatherings with songs and dances in some towns, and gompas are busy with prayers. In Rimbik and Maneybhanjan, you may be invited for tea if you are staying with a family. Remember that February is also deep winter on the ridge, with snow likely above Tonglu, so combine a Losar visit with a lower-altitude stay.
tips: Dates move every year with the lunar calendar; check this year's Sonam Lhosar and Gyalpo Losar dates before planning.
If invited into a home, accept a little food or tea and greet elders first; a small gift of fruit or sweets is appropriate.
Expect some shops and jeeps to stop for a day or two around Losar; plan transport with slack.

faqs.q: When is Losar celebrated in the Darjeeling hills?
faqs.a: There are two main Losars. Tamang Sonam Lhosar usually falls in late January or February, and Sherpa Gyalpo Losar, the Tibetan new year, usually in February or early March. Both follow the lunar calendar, so dates change every year; check current dates before you travel.

Losar is mainly a family and community festival. Visitors can watch prayers at gompas and public gatherings respectfully, and those staying in homestays may be invited to share food. Do not walk into private homes or ceremonies uninvited.

faqs.q: What food is eaten at Losar?
faqs.a: Khapse, crisp fried pastries in many shapes, are the signature new year food. Families also prepare meat dishes, rice, and home-made drinks such as chhang. Sweets and fruit are offered at the gompa and to guests.

faqs.q: Is Losar a good time for the Sandakphu trek?
faqs.a: It falls in deep winter, when snow is common above Tonglu and the Land Rover track may close. Experienced, well-equipped trekkers can still go, but plan extra days. For many visitors, a Losar stay in Rimbik or Maneybhanjan plus a short trip to Tumling works better.

name: Dashain and Tihar on the ridge
when: Sep–Nov: Dashain (15 days, ending Vijaya Dashami), then Tihar about three weeks later
summary: Dashain and Tihar, the biggest festivals of the Nepali-speaking hills, fall in October and early November, right at the start of the clear trekking season. Families gather for tika blessings at Dashain, then light lamps, honour crows, dogs and cows, and sing deusi-bhailo door to door at Tihar.
body: Dashain, celebrated in the Darjeeling hills and Nepal as the Nepali-speaking world's greatest festival, runs for fifteen days around the Durga Puja season. Barley shoots called jamara are sown in the first days. On Vijaya Dashami, the tenth day, elders place tika, a paste of rice, curd and red colour, on the foreheads of younger relatives, tuck jamara behind their ears and give blessings and money. Families travel long distances to be together.

Tihar follows about three weeks later and lasts five days. Crows are fed on the first day, dogs garlanded and honoured on the second, cows on the third, when Lakshmi Puja also lights every house with lamps. On the last day, Bhai Tika, sisters bless brothers with seven-coloured tika and marigold garlands. In the evenings, groups go door to door singing deusi and bhailo songs, collecting small gifts.

For trekkers, these festivals mean two things. First, villages like Maneybhanjan and Rimbik are full of families, swings, music and lights, and you may be offered sel roti, the ring-shaped festival bread. Second, many guides, drivers and lodge families take a few days off and hill transport is crowded with holiday travellers, so book Land Rovers, guides and jeep seats early.
tips: Check Dashain and Tihar dates when planning October treks; guides and jeeps may be scarce on the main days.
Expect higher demand and some higher prices on the ridge during the Puja and Dashain holidays; book huts and lodges early.
If deusi-bhailo singers come to your lodge, a small gift of ₹50–100 is customary and appreciated.

faqs.q: When are Dashain and Tihar celebrated?
faqs.a: Dashain falls in late September or October, ending with Vijaya Dashami, and Tihar comes about three weeks later in October or early November. Both follow the lunar calendar, so dates vary each year. Check current dates before you travel.

faqs.q: Do Dashain and Tihar affect the Sandakphu trek?
faqs.a: Yes. They coincide with peak trekking season and Indian holiday travel, so lodges and Land Rovers fill up and some guides take days off on the main festival days. Book ahead and allow flexibility.

During Tihar, groups of children and young people go from house to house singing traditional deusi and bhailo songs, blessing the household and receiving small gifts of money, food or sweets. It happens in the evenings in villages and towns across the hills.
Tika is a family blessing given by elders to relatives. Guests staying with a family are sometimes offered tika as a gesture of welcome. Accept respectfully if offered, but do not ask for it.
